title: At the shop: prices, quantities and "there isn't any"
goal: Shop with confidence: ask prices, give quantities, and say that something isn't there — which in Russian means yet another change of noun ending.
bekal: use много, мало, немного with the right form
say "there isn't any" with нет + genitive
name the usual packs and measures in Russian shops

dialogs.title: Диалог — The weekly shop
dialogs.intro: Ani is shopping at a small store near the dorm. Watch the nouns change their endings three times: after a number, after много, and after нет.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Hello! How much is the bread?

lines.speaker: Продавец:
lines.id: The dark one is 45 rubles, the white one 50.
lines.literal: black — forty — five — rubles, white — fifty.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: One dark, please. And is there any milk?
lines.literal: one — black, please. and — milk — is-there?

lines.speaker: Продавец:
lines.id: It's like milk, but sour. Very healthy.
lines.literal: this — like — milk, but — sour. very — useful.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: OK, just one. And how much are the apples?
lines.literal: good, let's — one. and — how-much — cost (pl) — apples?

lines.speaker: Продавец:
lines.id: A hundred and twenty a kilo.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Half a kilo, please. How much is it all together?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Here you go. Could I have a bag?

lines.speaker: Продавец:
lines.id: A bag is five rubles. Will you take one?

notes: **Нет + genitive means "there isn't any".** ⚠️ *Молока нет* is literally "of-milk there-is-none", and the milk must go into the genitive: молок**о** → молок**а**. Compare *Молоко есть* (there's milk), where the form is normal. So as soon as something is declared absent, its ending changes. It's the same pattern as *У меня нет брата* in Unit 4.

**Сколько стоит for one item, сколько стоят for several.** *Сколько стоит хлеб?* (singular) but *Сколько стоят яблоки?* (plural). Just like English "how much is" vs "how much are". Russians will understand you if you mix them up — but it's easy to get right.

**Рубль / рубля / рублей follow the number rule from Unit 7.** 1 рубль, 2–4 рубля, 5+ рублей. Since prices are almost always above five, the form you'll hear most is **рублей**. In everyday speech Russians often drop it altogether: *Сто двадцать* — a hundred and twenty, full stop.
**Что это такое? is more curious than Что это?** The added такое gives it a "what on earth is that?" tone. Very handy in Russian shops, where you'll meet plenty of things you've never seen at home.

**Давайте means "let's", and in a shop it means "I'll take".** *Давайте один* — I'll take one. *Давайте два килограмма* — two kilos, then. The familiar form is **давай**. It's also used to suggest things: *Давай пойдём!* — let's go!
**За means "per" or "for" when giving prices.** *Сто двадцать за килограмм* — 120 per kilogram. *Сколько за всё?* — how much for everything?
**A пакет isn't free, anywhere in Russia.** The cashier will ask *Пакет нужен?* (need a bag?) and add five to twenty rubles to the bill. The short answers are *Да, нужен* or *Нет, спасибо*.

grammars.title: Three places the genitive shows up in a shop
body: After the nominative, the genitive is the case you'll meet most. In this unit it appears in three places at once.

head: Appears after
Example
Meaning
rows: много книг, мало времени, немного сахар**а**
many books, little time, a little sugar

after: Genitive singular endings: masculine & neuter → **-а/-я** (хлеб → хлеба, молоко → молока), feminine → **-ы/-и** (вода → воды, Москва → Москвы).
⚠️ The genitive **plural** is much more complicated and you don't need to master it at A1. Just recognize the few forms you'll meet most in shops: рублей, книг, яблок, денег, лет, человек.

grammars.title: A lot and a little
body: All these words are followed by the genitive, so the noun always changes.

head: Русский
Say it
Meaning
Example
rows: много работы — a lot of work

after: ⚠️ **мало** and **немного** both mean "little", but their tone is opposite — like English "little" vs "a little". *Мало времени* complains — there's not enough time. *Немного времени* is neutral — there's a bit of time. Choosing wrong changes the meaning of the sentence.

sections.title: At the shop and the market

blocks.title: Phrases that save you at the checkout
items: **Сколько стоит?** — How much is it? You can say it while pointing, without naming the item.
**Это дорого.** — That's expensive. At the market (рынок) this opens the bargaining; in a supermarket it's just a statement.
**Можно скидку?** — Can I get a discount? ⚠️ Only at markets and small shops. Bargaining in a supermarket will be taken as a joke.
**У вас есть сдача?** — Do you have change? Useful because Russian sellers often ask for exact money: *Мельче нет?* (nothing smaller?).
**Картой можно?** — Can I pay by card? The answer is almost always yes; Russia is one of the least cash-dependent countries around.

exercises.prompt: Put into the form used after нет.
Put the words in the right order.

items: A hundred and twenty rubles a kilo.
How much is it all together?

answers: молока — хлеба — воды — времени — сахара — работы
рубль — рубля — рублей — рубля — рублей — рубль
Сколько стоит хлеб? — Молока нет. — Полкило, пожалуйста. — Можно пакет? — Это дорого.
Сколько стоит хлеб? — Молока нет. — Сто двадцать рублей за килограмм. — Полкило, пожалуйста. — Сколько всего? — Картой можно?
